# Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric dermatology > Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/Yk0nmT)

---

## Summary

Staphylococcal scalded <u>skin</u> syndrome (SSSS) is an acute <u>skin</u> condition caused by <u>exfoliative toxins</u> from <u>Staphylococcus aureus</u>. SSSS primarily affects <u>infants</u> and young children and most often follows a <u>staphylococcal infection</u> (e.g., <u>pharyngitis</u>, <u>bullous impetigo</u>), though the preceding infection may go unnoticed. Symptoms include <u>skin</u> tenderness, <u>erythema</u>, and <u>fever</u>, followed 1–2 days later by flaccid <u>blisters</u> and <u>superficial</u> <u>skin</u> sloughing that reveals moist red tissue (scalded appearance). <u>Mucous membranes</u> are spared. Diagnosis is clinical; <u>biopsy</u> is performed in the case of diagnostic uncertainty and reveals <u>intraepidermal</u> cleavage beneath the <u>stratum corneum</u>. Treatment involves <u>antibiotics</u>. SSSS generally heals without scarring.

---

## Epidemiology

* Rare condition (∼ 8 per 1,000,000 children) [[1]](/library/i1XJgC)

* Primarily affects <u>infants</u> and young children between 6 months and 5 years of age (peak <u>incidence</u>: 2–3 years) [[2]](/library/R1XlgC)

* Rare in adults: may occur in adults with predisposing conditions (e.g., impaired renal function or <u>immunosuppression</u>) [[3]](/library/QWbuOs)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>

* <u>Staphylococcus aureus</u> strains that produce exfoliative toxins

* <u>Exfoliative toxin A</u> and B have been shown to cleave <u>desmoglein</u>-1 in the granular layer of the <u>epidermis</u> → disruption of <u>keratinocyte</u> attachments [[4]](/library/jpa_6l)

* Route of infection: dissemination of toxins from a local infection

* Following a <u>staphylococcal infection</u> elsewhere (e.g., <u>skin</u>, mouth, nose, throat, <u>GI tract</u>, <u>umbilicus</u>). The initial infection may also be completely undetected.

* Following <u>bullous impetigo</u>





> [!NOTE]
> SSSS belongs to the spectrum of diseases mediated by specific staphylococcal toxins, which also includes <u>bullous impetigo</u>, <u>toxic shock syndrome</u> (<u>TSS</u>), and <u>Staphylococcus aureus</u> <u>food poisoning</u>. Unlike <u>TSS</u>, SSSS does not have systemic manifestations (involvement of, e.g., <u>liver</u>, <u>kidney</u>, <u>bone marrow</u>, <u>CNS</u>).

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Prodrome</u>: <u>fever</u>, <u>skin</u> tenderness, irritability [[5]](/library/ERd8Kp0)

* Cutaneous lesions [[5]](/library/ERd8Kp0)

* Initial manifestation

* <u>Erythematous</u> <u>macules</u> localized to face, neck, and <u>intertriginous areas</u>

* Perioral and periocular crusting

* Progression over 48 hours

* Flaccid, easily ruptured <u>bullae</u>

* Positive <u>Nikolsky sign</u>

* Widespread desquamation with moist red <u>skin</u> beneath (i.e., a “scalded” appearance)

* Crusting and/or fissuring of the <u>skin</u>

* Systemic illness: : <u>signs of hypovolemia</u> (e.g., <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>hypotension</u>), hypo- or <u>hyperthermia</u>

* Symptoms from the primary site of <u>S. aureus</u> infection, e.g.:

* <u>Bacterial conjunctivitis</u>

* <u>Bacterial sinusitis</u>

* <u>Impetigo</u>

* <u>Pharyngitis</u>





> [!TIP]
> Unlike <u>Stevens-Johnson syndrome</u> (<u>SJS</u>) and <u>toxic epidermal necrolysis</u> (TEN), SSSS spares <u>mucosal</u> membranes. [[5]](/library/ERd8Kp0)

## Diagnosis

SSSS is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>, typically supported by a history of a localized <u>S. aureus</u> infection and characteristic physical findings. <u>Laboratory studies</u> are performed in the case of diagnostic uncertainty. [[5]](/library/ERd8Kp0)




* <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[5]](/library/ERd8Kp0)

* <u>CBC</u>: normal or ↑ <u>WBCs</u>

* Bacterial cultures of potential sites of preceding <u>S. aureus</u> infection, e.g., urine, <u>nasopharynx</u>, <u>conjunctiva</u>  [[3]](/library/QWbuOs)[[5]](/library/ERd8Kp0)

* <u>Blood cultures</u>: typically positive for <u>S. aureus</u> in adults  [[3]](/library/QWbuOs)[[5]](/library/ERd8Kp0)

* <u>Skin biopsy</u> (confirmatory study)

* Indication: diagnostic uncertainty, e.g., to rule out <u>SJS</u> or TEN

* Findings [[3]](/library/QWbuOs)

* <u>Superficial</u> <u>intraepidermal</u> cleavage beneath the <u>stratum corneum</u>

* No inflammatory cell infiltrate

* No <u>keratinocyte</u> <u>necrosis</u>

---

## Differential diagnoses

### Severe exfoliative <u>skin</u> conditions




| Differential diagnoses of severe exfoliative skin conditions |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Staphylococcal scalded <u>skin</u> syndrome | <u>Stevens-Johnson syndrome</u> | <u>Toxic epidermal necrolysis</u> |
| Typical patient | <br>* Children < 6 years of age<br><br> | <br>* Adults<br><br> |  |
| Etiology | <br>* Infectious: <u>exfoliative toxins</u> (<u>S. aureus</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Delayed hypersensitivity reaction</u> triggered by medications or infections<br><br> |  |
| Clinical features | <br><br>* <u>Skin</u> sloughing<br><br>* Positive <u>Nikolsky sign</u><br><br>* Perioral <u>erythema</u> and crusting<br><br>* No <u>mucous membrane</u> involvement<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Skin</u> sloughing<br><br>* Positive <u>Nikolsky sign</u><br><br>* <u>Mucous membrane</u> involvement<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Affects < 10% of <u>total body surface area</u><br><br> | <br>* Affects > 30% of <u>total body surface area</u><br><br> |  |  |
| <br><u>Biopsy</u> [[3]](/library/QWbuOs)[[6]](/library/GPdBTJ0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Superficial</u> <u>intraepidermal</u> cleavage beneath the <u>stratum corneum</u><br><br>* No inflammatory cell infiltrate<br><br>* No <u>keratinocyte</u> <u>necrosis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Keratinocyte</u> <u>necrosis</u><br><br>* Aparent subepidermal split with separation of the <u>dermal-epidermal junction</u><br><br>* Progression to full-thickness <u>epidermal</u> <u>necrosis</u><br><br>* Sparse perivascular lymphoid infiltrate<br><br><br> |  |





### Other exfoliative and <u>blistering</u> <u>skin</u> conditions [[5]](/library/ERd8Kp0)




* See “<u>Overview of blistering skin diseases</u>” and “<u>Rash</u>.”

* <u>Kawasaki disease</u>

* <u>Toxic shock syndrome</u>

* <u>Pemphigus vulgaris</u>

* <u>Erythema multiforme</u>

* <u>Second-degree burns</u>

* <u>Graft-versus-host disease</u>

* <u>Sunburn</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### <u>Antibiotic therapy</u> [[7]](/library/LMbw68)[[8]](/library/Bldz_J0)




* Patients without <u>MRSA risk factors</u>

* <u>Nafcillin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[7]](/library/LMbw68)

* OR <u>oxacillin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[7]](/library/LMbw68)

* Patients with <u>MRSA risk factors</u>: <u>Vancomycin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[7]](/library/LMbw68)





### <u>Supportive care</u> [[5]](/library/ERd8Kp0)




* <u>Goal-directed IV fluid therapy</u>: See “<u>Strategies for IV fluid therapy</u>.”

* <u>Wound care</u>, e.g., with nonadherent dressings and/or <u>emollients</u>

* <u>Antipyretic therapy</u>, e.g., <u>acetaminophen</u>

* Antipruritic therapy, e.g., <u>cetirizine</u>, <u>diphenhydramine</u>

* <u>Pain management</u>: See “<u>Oral analgesics</u>” and “<u>Parenteral analgesics</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>NSAIDs</u>, as they may decrease <u>renal excretion</u> of <u>exotoxins</u>. [[5]](/library/ERd8Kp0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Steroids</u> are contraindicated, as the etiology of SSSS is infectious. [[8]](/library/Bldz_J0)




### Disposition and monitoring [[9]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Admission is typically required; consider transfer to a <u>burn center</u> for severe disease.

* Monitor for acute complications, including:

* <u>Superinfection</u>, <u>septic shock</u>

* <u>Hypovolemic shock</u>

* <u>Hypothermia</u>

* Treat complications, e.g., with:

* <u>Electrolyte repletion</u>

* <u>Rewarming techniques</u>

* <u>Broad spectrum antibiotics</u> for <u>sepsis</u>

---

## Prognosis

* <u>Mortality rate</u> [[10]](/library/Npa-pl)

* In children: < 5%

* In adults: > 60%

* <u>Blisters</u> heal completely, without scarring, as <u>skin</u> cleavage is <u>intraepidermal</u>.

---
